cards.title: Build an in-house creator scouting team instead of hiring an agency
cards.summary: Staff a 15–25 person in-house team of scouts who resemble your customer avatar to source and manage TikTok/Instagram influencers directly, as Bloom does with 85% of spend on creators.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run influencer/creator acquisition through an agency, a freelancer, or an internal team for your store's top-of-funnel content.
steps: Define your customer avatar precisely (Bloom's is a young female fitness/lifestyle buyer). Use that avatar to write the scouting job spec, not a generic 'social media manager' spec.

Hire young interns/scouts who personally look like and live in the same culture as the avatar — Bloom's rationale is that they can judge native content and speak credibly to creators in those communities.
Give scouts a clear mandate: identify creators whose audience matches the avatar, open the conversation, and shepherd creative from brief to post.
Keep management in-house so creator relationships, rates and performance data stay with you rather than an agency.
Bloom allocates about 85% of spend to influencers and under 5% to Meta, which only works because the internal team can source and brief at volume.
Reassess staffing against output (views, creator count published) rather than headcount vanity.
Verify current platform tools and program rules before building process around them; interfaces and policies change.
caveats: This is a resource-heavy structure described by one fast-growing brand; smaller stores may start with 1–3 scouts before scaling to a 15–25 person team.
Do not copy the 85/5 spend split as a benchmark — it reflects Bloom's category and stage, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Use VPNs to break regional algorithm bubbles when sourcing creators
cards.summary: Bloom's scouts use VPNs to shift their own feed geography, surfacing localized creators such as a mom in Kansas or a policewoman in North Carolina who would never appear in a coastal-city feed.
cards.use_when: Your influencer sourcing pipeline keeps returning the same handful of urban creators and you need genuinely diverse, regionally distributed voices for acquisition content.
steps: Set up VPN access for each scout so they can appear to be browsing from different US states or regions.
Have scouts scroll and interact (follow, watch, like) long enough for the platform algorithm to rebuild a localized feed before they start saving creator profiles.
Log candidates in a shared sheet with region, follower count, engagement, audience demographics and content style so sourcing is auditable.
Deliberately target geographies that match your customer base rather than only major metros — this widens the pool and reduces rate competition among the same creators.
Repeat the sweep per region on a schedule so the pipeline doesn't dry up.
Confirm that using VPNs complies with platform terms and local rules, and keep the method for sourcing only — do not use it to misrepresent campaign performance.
caveats: Platform terms and algorithm behaviour change; verify current rules before institutionalising this.
Sourcing diversity does not guarantee audience match — demographic checks still needed before paying creators.

cards.title: Price flat creator fees by reverse-engineering a target CPM
cards.summary: Instead of paying per post arbitrarily, set creator flat fees from a target CPM derived from your paid-social benchmark — Bloom halves Meta's CPM (e.g. $20 Meta → $10 creator target) and claims sub-$2 CPM outcomes on some deals.
cards.use_when: You are negotiating or budgeting creator/influencer flat fees and need a defensible per-video price rather than gut feel.
steps: Establish your current paid-social benchmark CPM (e.g. Meta) using a recent, representative window.
Set the creator target CPM below that benchmark — Bloom's working rule is to target roughly half of Meta's CPM.
Pull each candidate creator's trailing 10-video average views as the expected impression base (not follower count).
Multiply expected views by the target CPM and divide by 1,000 to derive a maximum flat fee offer.
Negotiate from that number, adjusting up for creators whose audience matches precisely and down for mismatch.
Track delivered views per paid creator post and recalculate your actual CPM so future budgets reflect what you actually achieved, not what you hoped.
Verify current platform view-count definitions and CPM reporting in your ad accounts before relying on them as benchmarks.
caveats: Bloom has reportedly achieved sub-$2 CPMs — treat that as a case example, not a promised benchmark.
Trailing-10-video averages can overstate expected reach for breakout/one-off viral videos.

cards.title: Discount creator payouts for off-target audience demographics
cards.summary: Bloom adjusts flat fees down when a creator's audience skews away from the target customer — e.g. cutting pay 25% if 25% of the audience is male when the target is female.
cards.use_when: You are setting or renegotiating creator rates and need to price in audience-quality mismatch rather than only reach.
steps: Define your target customer's core demographic traits (gender, age band, region) that matter for conversion.
Request audience-demographic screenshots or third-party data from the creator covering the same period as the view average you are pricing.
Quantify the off-target share — Bloom's example reduces the fee by 25% when 25% of the audience is male versus a female target.
Apply the adjustment consistently across creators so pricing is defensible and not a one-off negotiation tactic.
Document the formula in your creator rate card so scouts and negotiators apply the same logic.
Recheck demographics after campaigns — audience composition shifts over time.
caveats: The 25%-for-25% figure is Bloom's illustrative adjustment, not a validated conversion formula.
Creator-provided demographic screenshots can be incomplete; use additional sources where possible.

cards.title: Run influencer marketing with no affiliate links or coupon codes
cards.summary: Bloom deliberately avoids attribution links and codes and optimises for pure top-of-funnel awareness, relying on an omni-channel halo rather than last-click tracking.
cards.use_when: You are designing the measurement approach for a creator programme and deciding whether to impose trackable links or codes on creators.
steps: Accept that the goal is reach and brand demand, and evaluate success on views, reach and downstream channel lift rather than per-link ROAS.
Let creators post natively without link-stuffing or code-reading, which Bloom argues preserves organic performance.
Watch omni-channel signals — Bloom describes TikTok Shop success coinciding with roughly 30% lifts on Amazon, Target and Walmart — as evidence of a halo effect.
Use controlled comparisons where you can (e.g. retailer sell-through before/after a creator spike, geographic or timing splits) to sanity-check the halo instead of claiming direct causation.
Combine with brand-search volume, new-customer share and retailer reorder patterns as supplementary demand indicators.
Verify current platform and retailer reporting capabilities before finalising your measurement stack.
caveats: The ~30% lift figure is Bloom's observed example, not a guaranteed result.
Without links or codes, individual creator ROI is hard to isolate; this approach suits brands willing to manage at portfolio level.

cards.title: Give creators total creative control and avoid a 'lame' brief
cards.summary: Bloom attributes performance to minimal briefs — creators are the experts in their own communities, so the brand supplies product and guardrails rather than scripts.
cards.use_when: You are writing creator briefs for a paid or organic acquisition campaign and deciding how prescriptive to be.
steps: State the non-negotiables in the brief: product facts, legal claims restrictions, required disclosure and shipping/logistics.
Leave hook, format, tone, pacing and editing to the creator — Bloom explicitly avoids over-directing.
Provide reference content and product context rather than a script to read.
Review for compliance and brand safety only; push back on substance only when claims are false or non-compliant.
Let creators post to their own accounts and treat strong organic posts as a pool you can later amplify as paid creative.
After publishing, record which creator-led angles performed and feed themes (not scripts) back into future briefs.
Confirm current platform disclosure rules for sponsored content before briefing creators.
caveats: Full creative freedom requires pre-vetted creators with accurate audience alignment — it is riskier with untested accounts.
Some products (regulated supplements, health claims) require tighter briefs than Bloom's fitness example.

cards.title: Expand TAM by moving from a niche product into saturated, no-education categories
cards.summary: Bloom started with niche products (booty bands, female pre-workout for lifting/anxiety) then stepped up to greens, protein and energy drinks — deliberately choosing saturated categories to avoid spending money on consumer education.
cards.use_when: You are planning the next product line or category expansion for your store and deciding whether to pioneer a new category or enter an existing one.
steps: List your current niche products and the size of their addressable audience.
Identify adjacent categories with large existing demand where customers already understand the product benefit (protein, energy drinks, greens in Bloom's case).
Assess how much education spend each new category would require — Bloom avoids categories where the consumer must be taught the need.
Differentiate inside the saturated category with a 'better for you' positioning rather than a wholly new concept.
Sequence launches from smaller adjacent categories to bigger ones to build operational capability with each step.
Validate the audience step with community feedback (Bloom sources flavor/product feedback from in-person crowds rather than the loudest online commenters) before committing inventory.
Confirm regulatory and labeling requirements for each new category before launch.
caveats: Saturated categories mean higher competitive ad costs and shelf/listing competition.
TAM expansion requires supply chain and marketing capacity to match; moving too fast can strain operations.

cards.title: Read community feedback from in-person crowds, not online loud minorities
cards.summary: Bloom sources product and flavor feedback from physical crowd interactions to avoid over-indexing on the vocal keyboard minority that skews online sentiment.
cards.use_when: You are deciding what flavours, variants or product changes to launch next and want a more representative signal than comment sections or reviews.
steps: Create opportunities to talk to representative customers in person — Bloom uses large events and sampling moments as the venue.
Ask direct, structured questions about flavours, formats and purchase intent rather than open social-media polling.
Record responses in a consistent format (tally sheet or short survey) so they can be compared across events.
Explicitly discount the loudest online voices as a minority and look for patterns across a broader, more demographically representative group.
Cross-check in-person findings against sales and reorder data before committing to a full production run.
Limit waste with a small test batch or limited drop before scaling the winning variant.
caveats: In-person feedback can under-represent customers who never attend events.
This is Bloom's approach, not a validated research method — combine with transactional data.

cards.title: Use 'validity marketing' language such as 'restock' to signal demand
cards.summary: Bloom reports that 'restock' is the most powerful word in its marketing — signalling proven demand and scarcity rather than making a fresh claim — and uses this to attract retail buyers and investors.
cards.use_when: You are writing PDP copy, launch emails or social announcements and want to leverage evidence of real demand instead of discount-led messaging.
steps: Track sell-through and restock events as verifiable facts — count actual restocks and reference them accurately.
Write marketing copy around social proof of demand: 'restocked 3 times', 'back after selling out', 'limited drop returning'.
Publish these signals on Instagram and other public channels so retail buyers, distributors and investors see the demand story, not just consumers.
Use the same language on PDPs, launch emails and paid creative so the message is consistent across touchpoints.
Only claim restocks that genuinely happened — false scarcity damages credibility with buyers and customers.
Review which 'validity' messages correlate with sell-through or buyer enquiries over time.
caveats: This relies on genuine scarcity and demand; fabricated restocks breach trust and may breach advertising rules.
The strongest-word opinion is Greg's, not a universal rule — test against your own audience.

cards.title: Host large free in-person events to generate years of digital content
cards.summary: Bloom stages expensive live events (such as taking over a diner in Austin and giving away free meals all weekend) primarily to capture digital B-roll and content that can be reused for years.
cards.use_when: You are planning brand activations or content production and considering whether an in-person event earns its cost through reusable assets.
steps: Design the event around content capture, not just attendance — agree the shot list, creators attending and footage needed before booking the venue.
Bring cameras and creators so the same event yields vertical social video, stills, UGC and paid-creative assets.
Treat the event cost as content production budget: Bloom's stated rationale is that the footage is reusable for years.
Use the event to collect customer feedback (flavours, product reactions) alongside content.
Distribute the assets across organic channels, paid creative, retail buyer decks and investor material.
Measure both direct attendance value and downstream asset usage to judge whether the spend paid back.
caveats: This is a high-cost tactic suited to brands with capital and inventory to spare; Bloom describes it as a 'wild bet'.
Content from a single event can date quickly — plan refresh shots.

cards.title: Enter strategic distribution partnerships to solve supply chain without selling the company
cards.summary: Bloom partnered with Nutrabolt (C4) and Dr Pepper for its beverage launch to gain supply chain, logistics and distribution capability while reportedly maintaining 70% ownership and tripling enterprise value.
cards.use_when: You are launching a heavy or complex product (e.g. beverages) and need distribution, logistics or manufacturing partners but want to keep control of your store and brand.
steps: Identify the specific bottleneck the partnership must solve — Bloom's was beverage supply chain, logistics and distribution, not marketing.
Shortlist partners with existing infrastructure in that bottleneck rather than generalist investors.
Structure the deal so you retain a meaningful ownership stake; Bloom reports keeping 70% while the partnership scaled enterprise value 3x.
Agree clear roles: who handles production, warehousing, retail distribution and brand control.
Model the economics of the partnership against the alternative of building distribution yourself or selling a larger stake.
Secure legal and financial advice on governance, exclusivity and exit terms before signing.
caveats: The 70% ownership and 3x enterprise value outcomes are specific to Bloom's deal; yours will differ.
Partnerships trade some control for speed and reach — audit governance terms carefully.

cards.title: Prove retail concept with one chain, then scale doors and protect POs with inventory
cards.summary: Bloom focused on Target to prove the concept, then expanded to roughly 50,000 doors, and deliberately overproduces inventory so it never misses a purchase order from a major retailer.
cards.use_when: You are planning offline retail distribution for your store and need to decide which chain to prove first and how much stock to hold.
steps: Pick one national retailer to prove the concept (Bloom names Target) rather than pursuing many chains at once.
Use sell-through data and the halo effect from your digital channels as the evidence to pitch further chains once proven.
Build relationships with the individual human buyer at each retailer rather than treating the retailer as an institution.
Hold extra inventory so you never miss a major purchase order — Bloom says it overproduces for exactly this reason.
Accept the carrying cost of overproduction as insurance against damaging a retail relationship and losing shelf space.
Monitor retail sell-through and reorder cadence so overproduction does not become stale stock.
caveats: Overproducing ties up working capital and risks obsolescence — Bloom's example reflects a large, funded operation.
The ~50,000 doors figure is a Bloom outcome, not a target for other brands.

cards.title: Humanise relationships with retail buyers to win shelf space
cards.summary: Bloom's retail success came partly from building a relationship with the specific buyer at the retailer rather than anonymous account management.
cards.use_when: You are preparing a buyer pitch or managing an existing retail account and want to strengthen the human relationship that determines shelf space.
steps: Identify the named buyer or category manager for your product area — not just the generic vendor portal.
Approach them as a person: learn their category pressures, targets and what a win looks like on their P&L.
Bring evidence of demand (velocity, restock history, digital halo, test-market results) in the format they use for internal review.
Maintain regular, useful contact between review cycles rather than only emailing when you need something.
Follow through on every operational commitment; reliability is the currency for expanded shelf space and more doors.
Ask about timing cycles for category reviews and plan pitching around them.
caveats: Relationships do not override commercial requirements — evidence of sell-through still drives decisions.
Buyers change roles; institutionalise the relationship across more than one contact where possible.

cards.title: Apply the '1+1=3' framework when evaluating partnership deals
cards.summary: Bloom evaluates strategic partnerships on whether the combination produces capability neither party could efficiently build alone — as C4/Dr Pepper solved distribution for the beverage launch.
cards.use_when: You are assessing a distribution, manufacturing or retail partnership and want a framework for whether it is genuinely additive.
steps: Write down the specific capability gap on your side (logistics, distribution, manufacturing, shelf access) and quantify the cost or time to build it internally.
Write down what the partner brings that you cannot easily replicate.
Test the combination: does the deal produce a result larger than the sum of both sides' standalone efforts, or is it just a logo?
Check alignment of incentives — does the partner profit when your product succeeds?
Structure terms that protect your brand control, ownership and ability to exit.
Model the enterprise value impact of the partnership against the dilution or control you give up.
caveats: '1+1=3' is Greg's framing, a heuristic rather than a formula.
Partnerships that solve distribution can also create dependency; keep an internal capability roadmap.

cards.title: Use TikTok Shop success as a digital-to-retail halo signal
cards.summary: Bloom tracks TikTok Shop sales as a demand engine whose success coincides with lifts on Amazon, Target and Walmart, without using affiliate links to model the effect.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much to invest in TikTok Shop versus other channels and want to account for its knock-on effect on retail and marketplace sales.
steps: Track TikTok Shop sales and view-through separately from your other channels.
Compare periods of TikTok velocity against Amazon, Target and Walmart sell-through to observe correlated lifts (Bloom cites roughly 30%).
Use those correlations with retail buyers as evidence of digital demand they can bank on for shelf placement.
Avoid relying solely on last-click attribution for TikTok Shop; use timing and geographic comparisons to estimate the halo.
Feed the findings back into budget allocation between social commerce and traditional paid channels.
Verify current TikTok Shop reporting and retailer data feeds before building your dashboard.
caveats: The ~30% lift is Bloom's observed example; correlation is not proof of causation.
Platform commerce features and reporting change frequently — re-verify before committing budget.

cards.title: Ask candidates which three brands they love and why in hiring
cards.summary: Bloom uses a simple interview question — name three brands you love and why — to assess taste, consumer instinct and brand literacy for ecommerce marketing roles.
cards.use_when: You are hiring for marketing, brand, creative or merchandising roles in your store and want a signal of consumer taste beyond a CV.
steps: Ask the candidate to name three brands they love and explain why, listening for specificity and consumer-level reasoning rather than generic praise.
Assess whether their answers reveal instinct about what makes brands work (product, packaging, community, culture) relevant to your category.
Use the answers to test cultural and aesthetic alignment with your customer avatar.
Pair the question with practical work samples or a short creative/sourcing exercise to avoid over-weighting conversation.
For core roles, weigh in-person presence — Bloom is deliberately anti-remote for core roles, requiring Austin or LA.
caveats: Taste questions are subjective and can introduce bias; use alongside structured, job-relevant assessment.
Bloom's anti-remote stance is company-specific and not universally right for ecommerce teams.

cards.title: Build founder personal brand to control deal flow and luck
cards.summary: Greg built a personal brand deliberately to generate inbound opportunities, relationships and high-level connections rather than relying on outbound.
cards.use_when: You want to attract retail buyers, investors, partners or senior hires to your ecommerce brand through the founder's visibility.
steps: Publish consistently about your brand's build — product decisions, restocks, retail wins — from the founder's own account.
Use that visibility to attract inbound deal flow (partners, investors, distributors) rather than cold outreach.
Route the attention back to the store by cross-posting product content and linking to launches.
Document milestones publicly (new retail doors, partnerships, restocks) so your track record is legible to buyers and investors.
Protect credibility by only publishing claims that are true and verifiable.
Review whether inbound opportunities and press actually increase over time and adjust effort accordingly.
caveats: Personal branding takes sustained time and is hard to attribute directly to sales.
Public claims create accountability — avoid overstating outcomes.

cards.title: Use creator content as a paid-social creative pool instead of agency-produced assets
cards.summary: Bloom's high creator volume across TikTok and Instagram (reportedly 15 billion+ views) supplies a pool of native creative that can be used and re-used for paid social.
cards.use_when: You are planning paid-social creative supply and deciding whether to commission creator content or build assets internally/with an agency.
steps: Commission creators at volume with native hooks so you accumulate a large bank of tested creative.
Flag top-performing organic posts as candidates for paid amplification rather than briefing entirely new paid scripts.
When amplifying, keep the native look and feel; heavy editing tends to reduce performance on TikTok and Reels.
Organise the creative library by hook, audience and format so you can match assets to paid audiences.
Track performance of creator-sourced creative versus in-house studio creative in paid channels.
Refresh the pool continuously, since creative fatigue sets in quickly on paid social.
Verify current paid amplification permissions and usage rights before repurposing creator content.
caveats: Amplifying creator content requires usage rights in the original agreement — sort this when contracting.
View-count totals are Bloom's reported outcome; your results will vary with budget and category.

cards.title: Step up TAM ceilings deliberately from niche subsets to mass market
cards.summary: Bloom's sequence — booty bands and female pre-workout for lifting/anxiety, then greens, then protein, then energy drinks — shows a deliberate ladder from niche audiences to mass-market categories.
cards.use_when: You are planning a multi-year product roadmap for your store and want to raise the addressable market ceiling with each launch.
steps: Map current products to their audience size and identify the ceiling of your existing niche.
Choose the next category up the ladder — bigger audience, adjacent to your current positioning, requiring less education than a pioneering category.
Check whether your existing brand and customer base can credibly stretch into the next category (fitness supplements → energy drinks in Bloom's case).
Launch with a differentiated 'better for you' angle in the new category rather than a generic entry.
Use community and event feedback to validate the new product before a full production commitment.
Review whether each new launch actually lifted overall addressable market and repeat purchase, not just new-customer count.
Confirm regulatory and labelling requirements when moving into new categories, especially food and beverage.
caveats: Each step up the ladder brings larger, better-funded competitors.
Expanding TAM too far from the original brand can confuse existing customers.

Analyze the Data:

Source: YouTube video "How Bloom Built the Playbook Every Founder Will Copy in 2026" (Interview with Greg, co-founder of Bloom).

Topics Covered:

Influencer Marketing (ORG/MCR/WLD): Bloom is known for building a massive in-house influencer program. 85% of spend is on influencers, less than 5% on Meta. Scaled to over 15 billion views on TikTok and Instagram.

Influencer Infrastructure: Uses young interns as "scouters" because they look like the avatar (the "Bloom Girl"). They use VPNs to change their algorithms geographically to find diverse influencers (e.g., a mom in Kansas, a police woman in North Carolina).

Financials/Compensation: Reverse engineers compensation from Meta CPMs. If Meta is $20 CPM, target $10 CPM for influencers. Has achieved sub-$2 CPMs. Pays influencers flat fees (sometimes six figures) based on trailing 10 video view averages. Modifies payouts based on audience demographics (e.g., cuts by 25% if 25% of the audience is male, when the target is female).

Attribution (MEA): No affiliate links, no coupon codes. Optimizing for pure top-of-funnel awareness. Mentions the "halo effect" where TikTok shop success feeds into 30% lifts on Amazon, Target, and Walmart.

Product/Brand strategy (BRD/PRD): Target TAM expansion. Started with a niche product (booty bands, female pre-workout for lifting/anxiety). Moved to greens, then protein, then energy drinks. Concept of making "better for you" products in saturated spaces. They don't want to spend money on education.

Creative strategy (MCR): "Do not give a lame product brief." Gives content creators total creative control because they are the experts in their communities.

Retail strategy (WLD/SET? Growth): Focus on Target to prove concept, which led to 50,000 doors. They overproduce inventory so they never miss a PO for major retailers. Advice: Build the relationship with the individual human/buyer at the retailer.

Wild Bets / PR / CXP (WLD/CXP): Using "validity marketing" ("restock is the most powerful word"). Showcasing success on Instagram to get retailers/investors calling them. Throwing massive in-person events (e.g., taking over a diner in Austin, giving away free meals all weekend) to capture digital content for years.

Partnerships: Formed a strategic partnership with Nutrabolt (C4) and Dr. Pepper to solve supply chain, logistics, and distribution for their beverage launch. Allowed them to maintain 70% ownership while 3x'ing enterprise value.

Hiring/Culture: Hiring the "Bloom girl". Multi-city offices, but anti-remote for core roles (must be in Austin or LA). Asking interviewees to name three brands they love and why.

Personal Branding: Greg built his personal brand to control luck, generate deal flow, and build high-level connections.

Module Guide Boundary Testing:

Is it 4 or more distinct modules?

ORG (Organic and Content): Sourcing TikTok influencers, managing a 15-25 person in-house influencer team without agencies, using VPNs to hack algorithms, creator freedom in briefs.

MCR (Paid Social Creative): Paying creators based on CPM formulas, using organic influencer content to drive 15 billion views.

MEA (Measurement and Economics): Pure top-of-funnel tracking without attribution links, recognizing the omni-channel halo effect, reverse-engineering flat payouts from trailing 10 video averages.

WLD (Wild Bets): In-person diner takeover stunts for digital B-roll, validity marketing ("restocked 3 times"), strategic partnership with C4/Dr. Pepper to solve distribution.

BRD (Brand): Moving at the speed of culture, expanding TAMs from niche to mass market (energy drinks).

Yes, this is definitively a 99-multi.
